summary.text: Faulhaber’s formula together with the finite-field power-sum congruence gives the von Staudt–Clausen valuation criterion: for even \(k\ge4\), \(v_p(B_k)=-1\) exactly when \(p-1\mid k\), and otherwise \(v_p(B_k)\ge0\). Applying this prime by prime shows for odd composite \(n\) that squarefreeness of the resulting denominator is equivalent to \(n\) being squarefree and \(p-1\mid n-1\) for every prime \(p\mid n\), hence to the all-bases Fermat condition by Korselt’s criterion; for even composites, \(B_{n-1}=0\) makes the denominator nonsquarefree, while the base \(n-1\equiv-1\pmod n\) also rules out that Fermat condition.

full_proof.text:
Let the Bernoulli numbers be denoted by \(B_r\), with the convention determined by
\[
 \sum_{x=0}^{M-1}x^r
 =\frac1{r+1}\sum_{i=0}^{r}\binom{r+1}{i}B_iM^{r+1-i}.
\]
For a rational number \(q\), write it in reduced form as
\[
 q=\frac{\operatorname{num}(q)}{\operatorname{den}(q)},
\]
where \(\operatorname{num}(q)\in\mathbb Z\), \(\operatorname{den}(q)\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), and the numerator and denominator are coprime. For \(n>0\), put
\[
 F_n=\frac{\operatorname{num}(B_{n-1})}{n}
      +\frac{\operatorname{den}(B_{n-1})}{n^2},
 \qquad a(n)=\operatorname{den}(F_n).
\]
We prove that, for every composite \(n\), \(a(n)\) is squarefree if and only if \(n\) is a Carmichael number.

Throughout, \(v_p\) denotes the \(p\)-adic valuation, applied to nonzero integers or rationals as appropriate. In particular, if \(x/y\) is reduced, then
\[
 v_p(x/y)=v_p(x)-v_p(y).
\]
When a quantity in an intermediate valuation estimate can be zero, the assertion will be phrased as “it is zero, or its valuation is at least the stated bound.” This avoids any dependence on a convention for \(v_p(0)\).

We first establish the Bernoulli-number facts that will be needed.

### 1. A valuation form of the von Staudt–Clausen theorem

We claim first that, for every prime \(p\) and every \(r\ge 0\),
\[
 v_p(B_r)\ge -1
\tag{1}
\]
whenever \(B_r\ne0\).

This follows by strong induction on \(r\). It is immediate for \(r=0\), since \(B_0=1\). Suppose \(r\ge1\), and assume the assertion for every smaller index. Apply Faulhaber’s formula with \(M=p\), and isolate the term with index \(i=r\). Since
\[
 \binom{r+1}{r}=r+1,

after division by \(r+1\) that term is \(pB_r\). Thus
\[
 pB_r=A-C,
\tag{2}
\]
where
\[
 A=\sum_{x=0}^{p-1}x^r
	ag{3}
\]
and
\[
 C=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}
 B_i\binom{r+1}{i}\frac{p^{r+1-i}}{r+1}.
\tag{4}
\]
For \(i<r\), set \(J=r+1-i\). The elementary binomial identity
\[
 \binom{r+1}{i}(r+1-i)=(r+1)\binom ri
\]
rewrites the corresponding summand in \(C\) as
\[
 B_i\binom ri\frac{p^J}{J}.
\tag{5}
\]
If this summand is nonzero, its valuation is
\[
 v_p(B_i)+v_p\!\binom ri+J-v_p(J).
\tag{6}
\]
The induction hypothesis gives \(v_p(B_i)\ge-1\), and the binomial coefficient has nonnegative valuation. Also, for every \(J\ge1\),
\[
 v_p(J)\le J-1.
\tag{7}
\]
Indeed, \(p^{v_p(J)}\mid J\), hence \(2^{v_p(J)}\le J\). If \(v_p(J)\ge J\), this would imply \(2^J\le J\), impossible for \(J\ge1\). Therefore every nonzero summand of \(C\) has valuation at least \(0\). A finite sum of rationals each having valuation at least \(0\) also has valuation at least \(0\), unless the sum is zero; this is the nonarchimedean inequality
\[
 v_p(x+y)\ge\min(v_p(x),v_p(y)).
\]
The number \(A\) is an integer, so it too is zero or has nonnegative valuation. Equation (2) therefore shows that \(pB_r\) is zero or has nonnegative valuation. If \(B_r\ne0\), then
\[
 v_p(B_r)+1=v_p(pB_r)\ge0,
\]
which proves (1).

We now sharpen this for even indices. Let \(r\ge4\) be even. In the correction sum (4), a nonzero summand cannot have \(i=r-1\): the index \(r-1\) is odd and at least \(3\), and the Bernoulli number of every odd index greater than \(1\) is zero. Thus a nonzero summand has \(i\le r-2\), so \(J=r+1-i\ge3\).

For every prime \(p\) and every \(J\ge3\), we have the stronger estimate
\[
 v_p(J)\le J-2.
\tag{8}
\]
For if \(v_p(J)\ge J-1\), then \(2^{J-1}\le J\), whereas \(2^{J-1}>J\) for \(J\ge3\). Combining (6), (1), and (8), each nonzero summand in \(C\) has valuation at least
\[
 -1+J-v_p(J)\ge1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 C=0\quad\hbox{or}\quad v_p(C)\ge1.
\tag{9}
\]

It remains to understand \(A\) modulo \(p\). The standard power-sum computation in the finite field \(\mathbb F_p\) gives
\[
 \sum_{x=0}^{p-1}x^r\equiv
 \begin{cases}
 -1\pmod p,&p-1\mid r,\\
 0\pmod p,&p-1\nmid r.
 \end{cases}
\tag{10}
\]
For completeness, the zero term contributes nothing because \(r\ge1\). The multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^\times\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\). If \(g\) is a generator, then
\[
 \sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p^\times}x^r
 =\sum_{j=0}^{p-2}g^{jr}.
\]
If \(g^r\ne1\), this geometric sum is zero; if \(g^r=1\), every term is \(1\), and the sum is \(p-1=-1\) in \(\mathbb F_p\). Moreover, \(g^r=1\) exactly when \(p-1\mid r\). This proves (10).

The integer \(A\) is positive, since the term \(x=1\) occurs. Therefore (10) implies
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 p-1\mid r&\implies v_p(A)=0,\\
 p-1\nmid r&\implies v_p(A)\ge1.
 \end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]
Combining (2), (9), and (11), we obtain the desired valuation criterion. If \(p-1\mid r\), then \(A\) has valuation \(0\), while \(C\) is zero or has valuation at least \(1\). Thus \(A-C\) has valuation exactly \(0\), so
\[
 v_p(B_r)+1=v_p(pB_r)=0,

i.e.
\[
 v_p(B_r)=-1.
\tag{12}
\]
If \(p-1\nmid r\), both \(A\) and \(C\) are zero or have valuation at least \(1\), so (2) gives
\[
 v_p(pB_r)\ge1

after excluding the zero case; hence
\[
 v_p(B_r)\ge0.
\tag{13}
\]
Thus, for every even \(r\ge4\) and every prime \(p\),
\[
 \boxed{
 \begin{aligned}
 p-1\mid r&\implies v_p(B_r)=-1,\\
 p-1\nmid r&\implies v_p(B_r)\ge0.
 \end{aligned}}
\tag{14}
\]
Notice also that \(B_r\ne0\): take \(p=2\), for which \(p-1=1\mid r\), and (12) gives \(v_2(B_r)=-1\).

Write such a \(B_r\) in reduced form as \(N/D\). Since \(N\) and \(D\) are coprime, for each prime \(p\), at least one of \(v_p(N)\) and \(v_p(D)\) is zero. Since
\[
 v_p(B_r)=v_p(N)-v_p(D),
\]
criterion (14) implies
\[
 \boxed{
 \begin{aligned}
 p-1\mid r&\implies v_p(N)=0,\quad v_p(D)=1,\\
 p-1\nmid r&\implies v_p(D)=0.
 \end{aligned}}
\tag{15}
\]
Indeed, in the first case a difference of two nonnegative integers, at least one of which is zero, equals \(-1\), forcing the pair \((0,1)\). In the second case the difference is nonnegative, so coprimality rules out a positive denominator valuation.

### 2. Squarefree denominators and rational valuations

We use two elementary facts.

First, a nonzero positive integer \(m\) is squarefree if and only if
\[
 v_p(m)\le1
\tag{16}
\]
for every prime \(p\). This is immediate from unique prime factorization.

Second, if \(q=X/Y\) is a reduced rational number with \(Y>0\), then for every prime \(p\),
\[
 v_p(Y)\le1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v_p(q)\ge-1.
\tag{17}
\]
To see this, coprimality says that either \(v_p(X)=0\) or \(v_p(Y)=0\). If \(v_p(Y)>0\), then \(v_p(X)=0\) and \(v_p(q)=-v_p(Y)\); if \(v_p(Y)=0\), then \(v_p(q)=v_p(X)\ge0\). The assertion follows. It also holds for \(q=0\), whose reduced denominator is \(1\).

Combining (16) and (17),
\[
 \operatorname{den}(q)\text{ is squarefree}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 v_p(q)\ge-1\text{ for every prime }p.
\tag{18}
\]

### 3. The local analysis of \(F_n\) for odd composite \(n\)

Suppose now that \(n\) is odd and composite. Then \(n\ge5\), so
\[
 r=n-1

a is even integer at least \(4\). Write
\[
 B_{n-1}=\frac ND
\]
in reduced form. Thus
\[
 F_n=\frac Nn+\frac D{n^2}.
\tag{19}
\]
Fix a prime \(p\), and put
\[
 w=v_p(n).
\]
Let
\[
 T_1=\frac Nn,\qquad T_2=\frac D{n^2}.
\]
Both are nonzero because \(B_{n-1}\ne0\) and \(D>0\), and
\[
 v_p(T_1)=v_p(N)-w,
 \qquad
 v_p(T_2)=v_p(D)-2w.
\tag{20}
\]
We prove the key equivalence
\[
 \boxed{
 v_p(F_n)\ge-1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \bigl(w\le1\ \text{ and }\ [p\mid n\Rightarrow p-1\mid n-1]\bigr).}
\tag{21}
\]
There are two main cases.

**Case 1: \(p-1\mid n-1\).** By (15),
\[
 v_p(N)=0,
 \qquad
 v_p(D)=1.
\]
Hence
\[
 v_p(T_1)=-w,
 \qquad
 v_p(T_2)=1-2w.
\tag{22}
\]
If \(w=0\), both valuations are nonnegative, so the valuation of their sum is at least \(0\), unless the sum is zero, in which case its denominator is \(1\) and there is no problem. If \(w=1\), both valuations equal \(-1\), so the nonarchimedean inequality gives \(v_p(F_n)\ge-1\), again with the zero sum harmless. Thus \(w\le1\) implies the left side of (21).

If \(w\ge2\), then
\[
 1-2w<-w.
\]
When two nonzero rationals have unequal \(p\)-adic valuations, the valuation of their sum is exactly the smaller one. Therefore
\[
 v_p(F_n)=1-2w\le-3<-1.
\]
Thus in this case \(v_p(F_n)\ge-1\) holds exactly when \(w\le1\). The divisibility implication on the right side of (21) is automatically true because \(p-1\mid n-1\) is already assumed.

**Case 2: \(p-1\nmid n-1\).** By (15), \(v_p(D)=0\), while \(v_p(N)\ge0\). If \(w=0\), both terms in (20) have nonnegative valuation, so \(v_p(F_n)\ge0\), unless the sum is zero, which is again harmless.

If \(w\ge1\), then
\[
 v_p(T_2)=-2w,
 \qquad
 v_p(T_1)=v_p(N)-w\ge-w,

a and hence
\[
 v_p(T_2)<v_p(T_1).
\]
It follows that
\[
 v_p(F_n)=v_p(T_2)=-2w\le-2<-1.
\]
Thus in this case \(v_p(F_n)\ge-1\) holds exactly when \(w=0\), i.e. when \(p\nmid n\). That is precisely equivalent to the right side of (21), because if \(p\mid n\), the required implication would demand the divisibility \(p-1\mid n-1\), contrary to the present case. This proves (21).

By (18), \(a(n)=\operatorname{den}(F_n)\) is squarefree exactly when (21) holds for every prime \(p\). The first component, \(v_p(n)\le1\) for every prime \(p\), says exactly that \(n\) is squarefree. The second component says that every prime divisor \(p\) of \(n\) satisfies \(p-1\mid n-1\). Therefore, for every odd composite \(n\),
\[
 \boxed{
 a(n)\text{ is squarefree}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n\text{ is squarefree and }(p-1)\mid(n-1)
 \text{ for every prime }p\mid n.}
\tag{23}
\]

### 4. Korselt’s criterion

We now relate the right side of (23) to the Carmichael property.

For \(n\ge1\), let \(\lambda(n)\) be the exponent of the finite group \((\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^\times\): it is the least positive integer \(L\) such that \(u^L=1\) for every unit \(u\) modulo \(n\). By the defining property of a group exponent,
\[
 u^e=1\text{ for every }u\in(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^\times
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \lambda(n)\mid e.
\tag{24}
\]
A residue represented by \(b\) is a unit modulo \(n\) exactly when \(\gcd(b,n)=1\). Consequently,
\[
 b^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod n\text{ for every }b\text{ coprime to }n
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \lambda(n)\mid n-1.
\tag{25}
\]

We prove the needed form of Korselt’s criterion:
\[
 \boxed{
 \lambda(n)\mid n-1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n\text{ is squarefree and }p-1\mid n-1
 \text{ for every prime }p\mid n.}
\tag{26}
\]

We use the standard structure of unit groups modulo prime powers and the Chinese remainder theorem. For a prime \(p\),
\[
 \lambda(p)=p-1.
\tag{27}
\]
This follows because \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^\times\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\). Also,
\[
 p\mid\lambda(p^2).
\tag{28}
\]
For odd \(p\), the unit group modulo \(p^2\) has exponent \(p(p-1)\), so this is immediate; for \(p=2\), \(\lambda(4)=2\). More generally, if \(d\mid n\), reduction modulo \(d\) shows that
\[
 \lambda(d)\mid\lambda(n).
\tag{29}
\]
Equivalently, this also follows from the prime-power decomposition below. Finally, if
\[
 n=\prod_{p\mid n}p^{e_p},
\]
the Chinese remainder theorem gives
\[
 (\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^\times
 \cong\prod_{p\mid n}(\mathbb Z/p^{e_p}\mathbb Z)^\times,

a and the exponent of a finite direct product is the least common multiple of the exponents of its factors. Hence
\[
 \lambda(n)=\operatorname{lcm}_{p\mid n}\lambda(p^{e_p}).
\tag{30}
\]

Suppose first that \(\lambda(n)\mid n-1\). If \(p^2\mid n\) for some prime \(p\), then by (28), (29), and the hypothesis,
\[
 p\mid\lambda(p^2)\mid\lambda(n)\mid n-1.
\]
But \(p^2\mid n\) also gives \(p\mid n\). Thus \(p\) divides both \(n\) and \(n-1\), and hence divides \(1\), a contradiction. No prime square divides \(n\), so \(n\) is squarefree. Furthermore, if \(p\mid n\), then by (27) and (29),
\[
 p-1=\lambda(p)\mid\lambda(n)\mid n-1.
\]
This proves the forward implication in (26).

Conversely, suppose that \(n\) is squarefree and that \(p-1\mid n-1\) for every prime \(p\mid n\). Squarefreeness means every exponent \(e_p\) in (30) is \(1\). Therefore, using (27),
\[
 \lambda(n)=\operatorname{lcm}_{p\mid n}(p-1).
\]
Each number \(p-1\) in this least common multiple divides \(n-1\), so their least common multiple divides \(n-1\). Thus \(\lambda(n)\mid n-1\), proving (26).

Combining (25) and (26), we obtain Korselt’s criterion in its usual form: a composite integer \(n\) is a Carmichael number exactly when it is squarefree and \(p-1\mid n-1\) for every prime divisor \(p\) of \(n\).

It follows at once from (23) that for every odd composite \(n\),
\[
 a(n)\text{ is squarefree}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n\text{ is a Carmichael number}.
\tag{31}
\]

### 5. Even composite numbers

It remains to handle even composites. Let \(n\) be even and composite. Then \(n\ge4\), and \(n-1\) is odd and greater than \(1\). Bernoulli numbers of odd index greater than \(1\) vanish, so
\[
 B_{n-1}=0.
\]
In reduced form, \(0=0/1\), and therefore
\[
 F_n=\frac0n+\frac1{n^2}=\frac1{n^2}.
\tag{32}
\]
Since \(2\mid n\),
\[
 v_2(F_n)=-2v_2(n)\le-2.
\]
Equivalently, the denominator \(n^2\) contains at least \(2^2\), so \(a(n)\) is not squarefree.

An even composite \(n\) also cannot satisfy the Carmichael all-bases condition. Take
\[
 b=n-1.
\]
Then \(\gcd(n-1,n)=1\), while \(b\equiv-1\pmod n\). Since \(n-1\) is odd,
\[
 b^{n-1}\equiv(-1)^{n-1}\equiv-1\pmod n.
\]
If this were congruent to \(1\), then \(n\mid2\), impossible because \(n\ge4\). Thus every even composite number fails both properties: \(a(n)\) is not squarefree, and \(n\) is not Carmichael. Hence the desired equivalence also holds for even composite \(n\).

Every integer is either odd or even. Combining the odd-composite result (31) with the even-composite argument proves that for every composite number \(n\),
\[
 \boxed{\ a(n)\text{ is squarefree if and only if }n\text{ is a Carmichael number}.\ }
\]
Equivalently, for every natural number \(n\), the conjunction “\(n\) is composite and \(a(n)\) is squarefree” is equivalent to “\(n\) is a Carmichael number,” since being composite is part of the definition of a Carmichael number.
